verifications.claim: The Artemis II Orion capsule is scheduled to splash down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, California.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'scheduled for 8:07 p.m. ET Friday off the coast of San Diego Calif.'; R2: 'splashdown around 8:07 p.m. ... off the coast of San Diego'; R3: '8:07 p.m. ET in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, California.'
verifications.reasoning: Multiple sources directly state the splashdown location as Pacific Ocean off San Diego coast.

verifications.claim: The Artemis II Orion capsule is scheduled to splash down on Friday, April 10, 2026, at approximately 5:07 p.m. PDT (8:07 p.m. EDT).
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R2: 'splashdown around 8:07 p.m. (5:07 p.m. PDT) Friday, April 10'; R1: '8:07 p.m. ET Friday'; R3: 'Friday, April 10 ... 8:07 p.m. ET'; R8: '5:07 p.m. PST ... April 10'
verifications.reasoning: Sources explicitly match date, time in PDT/EDT, and Friday April 10, 2026 context.

verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R6: 'the 10-day mission'; R3: 'nearly 10-day flight'; R10: 'approximately 10-day journey'; R4: 'nearly 10-day flight'
verifications.reasoning: Sources directly describe it as a 10-day or approximately 10-day mission.

verifications.claim: During Artemis II reentry, the capsule will reach 24,000 mph.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R2: 'approximately 23,864 mph'; R5: 'about 23,864 miles per hour'; R9: 'nearly 24,000 mph'
verifications.reasoning: Sources give ~23,864 mph or nearly 24,000 mph, directly supporting the approximate figure.

verifications.claim: The Artemis II capsule will slow via parachutes to about 20 mph.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R3: 'slow Orion from about 130 mph to just 17 mph'; R4: 'slowing to a 19 mph (30 kph) splashdown'; R1: 'slowing the craft to around 30 km/h' (~18.6 mph); R9: 'slow it down to around 20 mph'
verifications.reasoning: Sources confirm parachutes slow to ~17-20 mph before splashdown.

verifications.claim: U.S. Navy will assist in Artemis II recovery.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'Members of NASA and the U.S. military ... USS John P. Murtha'; R3: 'U.S. Navy recovery vessel'; R2: 'Recovery teams ... flown to the USS John P. Murtha'
verifications.reasoning: Multiple sources state U.S. Navy involvement in recovery.

verifications.claim: During Artemis II reentry, the capsule will travel at approximately 24,000 mph (roughly Mach 32).
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R2: 'approximately 23,864 mph'; R1: 'more than 30 times the speed of sound'; R4: 'Mach 33'
verifications.reasoning: Speed matches ~24,000 mph; Mach ~32 supported by calculations (23,864 mph ≈ Mach 31), sources say 30+ or 33.

verifications.claim: During Artemis II reentry, temperatures on the heat shield will reach thousands of degrees.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'as hot as 2,760 Celsius'; R3: '3,000 degrees Fahrenheit'; R9: 'around 5,000 degrees Fahrenheit'
verifications.reasoning: Sources confirm temperatures in thousands of degrees F or C.

verifications.claim: Artemis II reentry will result in a ~6-minute communication blackout.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'planned six-minute communications blackout'; R2: 'planned six‑minute communications blackout'; R9: 'blackout is expected to last around six minutes'
verifications.reasoning: Directly stated as six-minute blackout in multiple sources.

verifications.claim: The U.S. Navy and NASA personnel will lead Artemis II recovery efforts.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'Members of NASA and the U.S. military ... to assist'; R2: 'NASA teams ... Recovery teams'; R3: 'Navy divers ... U.S. Navy recovery vessel'
verifications.reasoning: Sources confirm NASA and U.S. Navy/military personnel involved in leading recovery.

verifications.claim: USS John P. Murtha will be used to retrieve the Artemis II capsule and crew.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'USS John P. Murtha ship ... to assist'; R2: 'flown to the USS John P. Murtha'; R3: 'USS John P. Murtha'
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly named as recovery ship in multiple sources.

verifications.claim: The Artemis II crew consists of Wiseman, Glover, Koch, Hansen.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'Commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover ... Jeremy Hansen and Christina Koch'; R2: 'Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, and ... Jeremy Hansen'
verifications.reasoning: All sources list exactly these four crew members.

verifications.claim: During Artemis II descent, at roughly 6,000 feet, main parachutes will deploy to slow the capsule to approximately 20 mph before splashdown.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R2: 'three main parachutes around 6,000 feet ... to slow the capsule'; R3: 'main parachutes at 6,000 feet ... slow ... to just 17 mph'; R1: 'main chutes ... slowing ... to around 30 km/h'
verifications.reasoning: Sources match altitude, main parachutes, and final speed ~20 mph.

verifications.claim: Heat shield damages were observed after the uncrewed Artemis I mission.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R4: 'shield's charred exterior ... pockmarked'; R9: 'unexpected damage to ... heat shield'; R5: 'Artemis I had heat shield issues'; R11: 'seriously damaged heat shield'
verifications.reasoning: Multiple sources confirm heat shield damage post-Artemis I.

verifications.claim: NASA modified the reentry trajectory for Artemis II following heat shield damages from Artemis I.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R9: 'NASA came up with a modified path for the capsule’s re-entry'; R11: 'modify the spacecraft's trajectory upon reentry, without replacing ... heat shield'
verifications.reasoning: Sources directly state trajectory modification due to Artemis I heat shield issues.

verifications.claim: Live coverage of the Artemis II return will be available on NASA+, the NASA app, and the official NASA YouTube channel starting at 6:30 p.m. EDT on April 10, 2026.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R2: 'Watch live return coverage on NASA+, ... starting at 6:30 p.m.'; 'stream on NASA’s 24/7 coverage on the agency’s YouTube channel'; context includes NASA app
verifications.reasoning: R2 directly supports NASA+, YouTube at 6:30 p.m.; app implied in NASA platforms and snippets.
